stem: Match the consistency theory in List-I with its core idea in List-II.
listII: Inconsistency between cognitions produces aversive arousal that motivates change
Triadic P-O-X relationships: balanced vs unbalanced states
Persuasion produces change toward a midpoint (assimilation)
why: Heider's balance theory—triadic P-O-X relationships (1-B). Congruity theory—change toward a midpoint (2-C). Cognitive dissonance—inconsistency produces aversive arousal (3-A).

optWhy.A: Correct. 1-B, 2-C, 3-A.
optWhy.B: Balance theory is not inconsistency arousal.
optWhy.C: Congruity is not triadic P-O-X; dissonance is not midpoint.
optWhy.D: Congruity is not triadic P-O-X; dissonance is not midpoint.

stem: Adams's equity theory proposes that perceived fairness depends on:

options.text: The ratio of one's inputs to outcomes, compared with a referent other's ratio.

why: Equity theory holds that people compare their own inputs/outcomes ratio to a referent other's ratio; inequity (under- or over-reward) creates tension motivating restoration of equity.

optWhy.A: Correct. Fairness depends on the inputs/outcomes ratio compared with a referent.
optWhy.B: Absolute pay regardless of inputs is not equity theory.
optWhy.D: Obedience to the employer is unrelated.

stem: An employee who is over-rewarded relative to a referent experiences:

options.text: Over-reward inequity and may experience guilt or distort perceptions to restore equity.

why: Over-reward inequity (one's outcomes exceed inputs relative to a referent) can produce guilt and motivate restoration of equity, just as under-reward produces anger.

optWhy.A: Correct. Over-reward inequity can produce guilt and motivate equity restoration.
optWhy.B: Over-reward is a form of inequity.

stem: Responses to perceived inequity can include:

options.text: Restoring equity (changing inputs or outcomes), cognitively distorting perceptions, or leaving the relationship.

why: People respond to inequity by behaviourally restoring equity, cognitively distorting perceptions of inputs/outcomes, or psychologically/physically leaving the relationship.

optWhy.A: Correct. Responses include restoring equity, cognitive distortion, or leaving.
optWhy.B: Not only genetic changes.

stem: Equity theory differs from equality in that equity:

options.text: Allocates outcomes in proportion to inputs, whereas equality allocates the same to everyone regardless of inputs.

why: Equity distributes outcomes proportionally to inputs; equality distributes the same to all regardless of inputs.

optWhy.A: Correct. Equity = proportional to inputs; equality = same for all.
optWhy.B: Not genetic.
optWhy.C: Equity does not always produce identical outcomes.

stem: Social exchange theory views relationships as:

options.text: Transactions in which people weigh rewards against costs.
Groups with no rewards or costs.

why: Social exchange theory (Homans; Thibaut & Kelley) views social behaviour as exchanges in which people weigh rewards against costs.

optWhy.A: Correct. Relationships involve weighing rewards against costs.
optWhy.B: Not genetic contracts.

stem: In Thibaut and Kelley's interdependence theory, the comparison level (CL) is:

options.text: The standard against which outcomes are judged to determine satisfaction.
The standard against which outcomes are judged to determine whether to stay in the relationship.

why: The comparison level (CL) is the standard people use to judge whether outcomes are satisfactory; the comparison level for alternatives (CLalt) determines whether to stay or leave.

optWhy.A: Correct. CL judges satisfaction.
optWhy.B: CLalt (not CL) determines whether to stay or leave.

stem: A person stays in a relationship because outcomes exceed their comparison level and no better alternative exists. This reflects:

options.text: Satisfaction (outcomes above CL) and stability (no better alternative, outcomes above CLalt).

why: Staying because outcomes exceed CL (satisfaction) and no better alternative exists (outcomes above CLalt, stability) is the interdependence-theory account.

optWhy.A: Correct. Satisfaction plus stability explains staying.
optWhy.B: Not genetic.

stem: Equity theory and social exchange theory differ in that equity theory:

options.text: Adds a fairness criterion (proportional inputs/outcomes versus a referent) to the exchange framework.

why: Equity theory extends exchange by adding the criterion of fairness (inputs/outcomes ratio compared with a referent); pure exchange concerns rewards and costs.

optWhy.A: Correct. Equity adds fairness (proportionality versus a referent) to exchange.
optWhy.B: Not genetic.
optWhy.D: Equity does not ignore rewards and costs.

stem: Two groups compete for a promotion, and hostility arises; this is best explained by realistic conflict theory, whereas hostility arising merely from being categorised into 'blue' vs 'green' groups is best explained by social identity theory. The distinction is:

options.text: Realistic conflict theory requires competition over scarce resources; social identity theory requires only social categorisation.

why: RCT requires competition over scarce resources; SIT requires only social categorisation. They are distinct mechanisms, not genetic or obedience-based, and not the same theory.

optWhy.A: Correct. RCT needs resource competition; SIT needs only categorisation.
optWhy.B: Not genetic.

stem: A group feels deprived relative to a wealthier reference group despite rising absolute living standards, and protests. This is best explained by:

options.text: Relative deprivation theory (subjective deprivation versus a referent can motivate collective action).

why: Feeling deprived relative to a referent despite absolute gains is relative deprivation, which can motivate protest/collective action.

optWhy.A: Correct. Relative deprivation versus a referent motivates collective action.
optWhy.B: Objective deprivation is an absolute shortfall, not a relative comparison.

stem: A key strategy for reducing intergroup prejudice is:

options.text: Intergroup contact under optimal conditions (equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support).

why: Intergroup contact under optimal conditions (Allport's contact hypothesis: equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support) is a key strategy for reducing intergroup prejudice.

optWhy.A: Correct. Intergroup contact under optimal conditions reduces prejudice.
optWhy.B: Not genetic.

stem: Recategorisation (common ingroup identity model) involves:

options.text: Expanding the in-group boundary to include former out-group members.

why: Recategorisation involves expanding the in-group boundary to include former out-group members, creating a common ingroup identity and reducing bias.

optWhy.A: Correct. Recategorisation expands the in-group boundary to include former out-group members.
optWhy.B: Not genetic.

stem: Stereotype disconfirmation involves:

options.text: Encountering evidence that contradicts a stereotype.

why: Stereotype disconfirmation involves encountering evidence that contradicts a stereotype, which can reduce prejudice.

optWhy.A: Correct. Stereotype disconfirmation is encountering evidence that contradicts a stereotype.
optWhy.B: Not genetic.

stem: Consider the following statements about intergroup theories:
statements: I. Realistic conflict theory requires competition over scarce resources.
II. Social identity theory can produce in-group favouritism from mere categorisation.
III. Equity theory is the same as social exchange theory.
why: Statements I and II are true. Statement III is false because equity theory adds a fairness criterion to social exchange; they are related but not identical.

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements I and II are true; III is false.
optWhy.B: Statement III is false.

stem: Consider the following statements about prejudice reduction:
statements: I. Contact reduces prejudice most effectively under conditions of equal status, common goals, cooperation and institutional support.
II. Recategorisation creates a common ingroup identity that can reduce bias.
III. All prejudice can be eliminated by a single contact session.
why: Statements I and II are true. Statement III is false because a single contact session cannot eliminate all prejudice; effects depend on conditions and may be limited.

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements I and II are true; III is false.
optWhy.B: Statement III is false.

stem: Jurors' judgments can be influenced by a defendant's race, even when evidence is identical. This illustrates:

options.text: Prejudice and discrimination in legal judgements.

why: Jurors' judgments being influenced by a defendant's race despite identical evidence illustrates prejudice and discrimination in legal judgements.

optWhy.A: Correct. Prejudice and discrimination in legal judgements.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determination of guilt.

stem: In Sherif's autokinetic effect experiments, participants' individual estimates of a moving light converged toward a common group norm when tested together. The best interpretation is:

options.text: The light actually moved the same distance for everyone.
Informational influence can create a shared group norm in an ambiguous situation.
Participants were deliberately conforming to please the experimenter.
The autokinetic effect measures personality traits.

why: In an ambiguous situation (the stationary light appears to move), participants use others' estimates as information and converge on a group norm, demonstrating informational social influence. The light does not actually move, conformity is not merely impression management, and the task is not a personality measure.

optWhy.A: The autokinetic light is stationary; it does not actually move.
optWhy.B: Correct. Informational influence creates a shared group norm in ambiguity.
optWhy.C: Convergence reflects informational influence, not merely pleasing the experimenter.
optWhy.D: The autokinetic effect is a perceptual phenomenon, not a personality measure.

stem: Applying social psychology to reduce intergroup conflict in a workplace:

options.text: Introduce superordinate goals requiring cooperation between groups.

why: Introducing superordinate goals requiring cooperation between groups is a realistic conflict theory-based strategy to reduce intergroup conflict.

optWhy.A: Correct. Superordinate goals requiring cooperation reduce intergroup conflict.
optWhy.B: Not genetic.

stem: Social determinants of health include:

options.text: Social and economic conditions such as income, education, and social support that shape health.

why: Social determinants of health are the social and economic conditions (income, education, social support, etc.) that shape health outcomes.

optWhy.A: Correct. Social and economic conditions shape health.
optWhy.B: Genetic factors are not the only determinants.
optWhy.C: Individual behaviour is not the only determinant.
optWhy.D: Medical care is not the only determinant.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: The Health Belief Model proposes that health behaviour depends on:

options.text: Perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action, and self-efficacy.

why: The Health Belief Model includes perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers, cues to action, and self-efficacy as determinants of health behaviour.

optWhy.A: Correct. These are the HBM components.
optWhy.B: Genetic factors are not the only determinant.
optWhy.D: Social loafing is reduced effort in groups.

stem: A person intends to exercise regularly, has a favourable attitude toward exercise and believes important others approve, but lacks access to a gym. The theory that best accounts for the gap between intention and behaviour is:

options.text: The theory of reasoned action, which includes perceived behavioural control.
The theory of planned behaviour, which adds perceived behavioural control to the theory of reasoned action.

why: The theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen) extends the theory of reasoned action by adding perceived behavioural control, which explains why intention may not translate into behaviour when control (e.g., gym access) is lacking.

optWhy.A: TRA does not include perceived behavioural control; TPB does.
optWhy.B: Correct. TPB adds perceived behavioural control to TRA.
optWhy.C: Cognitive dissonance concerns inconsistency, not the intention-behaviour gap.
optWhy.D: Balance theory concerns triadic consistency, not behavioural control.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: The buffering hypothesis of social support proposes that:

options.text: Social support protects health by buffering the impact of stress.
Social support only works through obedience.

why: The buffering hypothesis holds that social support protects people from the adverse health effects of stress.

optWhy.A: Correct. Social support buffers the impact of stress on health.
optWhy.B: Social support does not always harm health.
optWhy.C: Social support is not genetically determined.
optWhy.D: Social support does not work through obedience.

stem: A person avoids seeking mental-health treatment because of fear of being labelled. This illustrates:

options.text: Stigma affecting health behaviour and help-seeking.

why: Avoiding treatment due to fear of labelling illustrates how stigma can undermine health behaviour and help-seeking.

optWhy.A: Correct. Stigma affects health behaviour and help-seeking.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Health communication applies persuasion principles to:

why: Health communication uses persuasion (source, message, audience) to promote health-related attitudes and behaviours.

optWhy.A: Correct. Health communication promotes health-related attitudes and behaviours through messages.
optWhy.B: Not genetic modification.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: A theory-based programme that changes attitudes, norms and perceived control to improve medication adherence is an example of:
why: Changing attitudes, norms and perceived control to improve adherence is a theory-based behaviour-change intervention.

optWhy.A: Correct. Theory-based behaviour-change intervention.
optWhy.B: Not genetic modification.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Cultural influences on health behaviour mean that:

options.text: Health beliefs and behaviours vary across cultural contexts and should be considered in interventions.
Health behaviour is genetically identical across cultures.
Culture has no effect on health.

why: Health beliefs, behaviours and help-seeking vary across cultural contexts, so interventions should be culturally sensitive.

optWhy.A: Correct. Health beliefs and behaviours vary across cultural contexts.
optWhy.B: Health beliefs and behaviours are not genetically identical across cultures.
optWhy.D: Obedience does not determine health behaviour.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Environmental attitudes and behaviour concern:

options.text: How people evaluate the environment and act to protect or harm it.

why: Environmental attitudes and behaviour concern people's evaluations of the environment and their actions to protect or harm it (pro-environmental behaviour).

optWhy.A: Correct. Evaluations of the environment and actions to protect or harm it.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determination.
optWhy.C: Not obedience to environmental laws only.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: A campaign tells residents that most neighbours recycle, increasing recycling. This uses:

options.text: Social norms (descriptive norms) to promote pro-environmental behaviour.

why: Describing what most neighbours do uses descriptive social norms to promote pro-environmental behaviour.

optWhy.A: Correct. Descriptive social norms promote pro-environmental behaviour.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Environmental stressors such as noise can impair psychological functioning.
reason: Noise can disrupt concentration, increase stress, and reduce task performance, especially when it is unpredictable and uncontrollable.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

why: Both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion: noise is an environmental stressor that impairs functioning via concentration disruption, stress, and reduced performance, especially when unpredictable and uncontrollable.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: The reason does explain the assertion.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Match the environmental-psychology concept in List-I with its description in List-II.
listII: The emotional bond between a person and a place
Adverse psychological effects of environmental conditions such as noise and crowding
The growth of cities and its social-psychological effects
Actions that minimise harm to the environment
why: Place attachment—emotional bond to a place (1-A). Environmental stress—adverse effects of conditions like noise/crowding (2-B). Urbanisation—city growth and effects (3-C). Pro-environmental behaviour—actions minimising environmental harm (4-D).

optWhy.A: Correct. 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D.
optWhy.B: Place attachment is not environmental stress.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: A household installs solar panels and reduces water use out of concern for the environment. This is:
why: Installing solar panels and reducing water use out of environmental concern is pro-environmental behaviour.

optWhy.A: Correct. Pro-environmental behaviour.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Eyewitness testimony is not always accurate and can be distorted.
reason: Memory is reconstructive, and post-event information can alter memory for an event (the misinformation effect).

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

why: Both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion: memory is reconstructive, and post-event information (Loftus's misinformation effect) can distort eyewitness memory.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: The reason does explain the assertion.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Match the eyewitness-memory concept in List-I with its description in List-II.
listII: Post-event information distorts memory for an event
A weapon draws attention, reducing memory for other details
Identifying a suspect from a lineup
Remembering an event that did not occur
why: Misinformation effect—post-event information distorts memory (1-A). Weapon focus—a weapon draws attention, reducing memory for other details (2-B). Line-up identification—identifying a suspect from a lineup (3-C). False memory—remembering an event that did not occur (4-D).

optWhy.A: Correct. 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D.
optWhy.B: Misinformation effect is not weapon focus.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: A sequential line-up (viewing suspects one at a time) tends to reduce:

options.text: Relative judgements and false identifications compared with simultaneous line-ups.

why: Sequential line-ups reduce relative judgements (comparing suspects to each other) and false identifications relative to simultaneous line-ups.

optWhy.A: Correct. Sequential line-ups reduce relative judgements and false identifications.
optWhy.B: Not all identifications.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: A suspect confesses to a crime they did not commit after prolonged, coercive interrogation. This illustrates:

options.text: A false confession, which can result from coercive interrogation and suggestibility.

why: A false confession is an admission to a crime not committed, which can result from coercive interrogation, suggestibility, and other pressures.

optWhy.A: Correct. A false confession can result from coercive interrogation and suggestibility.
optWhy.B: Not genetic guilt.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Jury decisions are influenced by social processes such as conformity and minority influence.
reason: Juries deliberate as groups, so majority pressure and consistent minorities can shape verdicts.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

why: Both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion: jury deliberation is a group process in which conformity and minority influence shape verdicts.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: The reason does explain the assertion.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
sub: Prejudice and discrimination in legal judgements
stem: Jurors' judgments can be influenced by a defendant's race, even when evidence is identical. This illustrates:

options.text: Prejudice and discrimination in legal judgements.

why: Jurors' judgments being influenced by a defendant's race despite identical evidence illustrates prejudice and discrimination in legal judgements.

optWhy.A: Correct. Prejudice and discrimination in legal judgements.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determination of guilt.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
sub: Psychology of criminal behaviour and justice
stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Social psychology contributes to understanding criminal behaviour and justice.
reason: Social-psychological research on aggression, attribution, and group processes informs how crime and justice are understood.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

why: Both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion: social psychology informs criminal behaviour and justice through research on aggression, attribution, and group processes.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: The reason does explain the assertion.

key: Psychology of criminal behaviour and justice

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
sub: Applications and limitations of social psychological research in law
stem: Consider the following statements about social psychology in law:
statements: I. Social psychology has informed eyewitness testimony, line-up identification, and jury decision-making.
II. Social-psychological findings always apply directly and without limitation in legal settings.
III. Legal settings have constraints (e.g., admissibility rules) that social psychology must consider.
why: Statements I and III are true. Statement II is false because findings do not always apply directly and without limitation; legal settings have constraints such as admissibility rules.

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements I and III are true; II is false.
optWhy.B: Statement II is false.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Match the concept in List-I with Loftus's contribution in List-II.
listII: Memory is rebuilt rather than reproduced like a recording
Post-event information can distort memory for an event
Research showing memory for witnessed events is fallible
Remembering events that did not happen
why: Misinformation effect—post-event information distorts memory (1-B). Eyewitness testimony—research showing memory for witnessed events is fallible (2-C). False memory—remembering events that did not happen (3-D). Reconstructive memory—memory is rebuilt rather than reproduced (4-A).

optWhy.A: Correct. 1-B, 2-C, 3-D, 4-A.
optWhy.B: Misinformation effect is not reconstructive memory.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: Consider the following statements about eyewitness testimony:
statements: I. Eyewitness confidence is only weakly related to accuracy.
II. Post-event misinformation can distort eyewitness memory.
III. Eyewitness testimony is always accurate.
why: Statements I and II are true. Statement III is false because eyewitness testimony is not always accurate.

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements I and II are true; III is false.
optWhy.B: Statement III is false.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
stem: In jury experiments, jurors exposed to inadmissible evidence (later told to ignore it) are still influenced by it. The best interpretation is:

options.text: Inadmissible evidence can have a persistent biasing effect despite judicial instructions to disregard it.

why: Jurors remain influenced by inadmissible evidence despite instructions to disregard it, showing a persistent biasing effect that legal safeguards do not fully eliminate.

optWhy.A: Correct. Inadmissible evidence can persistently bias jurors despite instructions.
optWhy.B: Jurors do not always follow judicial instructions.
optWhy.C: Genetic factors do not determine verdicts.

topic: Applied Social Psychology: Health, Environment and Law
sub: Applications and limitations of social psychological research in law
stem: Field experiments show that police line-up procedures using sequential presentation and double-blind administration reduce false identifications. The best interpretation is:

options.text: Procedural safeguards (sequential line-ups, double-blind administration) can reduce false identifications in applied legal settings.

why: Sequential presentation and double-blind administration are procedural safeguards that reduce false identifications, showing applied social psychology can improve legal procedures.

optWhy.A: Correct. Procedural safeguards reduce false identifications.
optWhy.B: Not all identifications are accurate.
optWhy.C: Genetic factors do not determine identifications.
optWhy.D: Obedience to police does not guarantee accuracy.

stem: Personal space is best defined as:

options.text: The physical region surrounding a person that they regard as their own and wish to keep free from intrusion.

why: Personal space is the invisible, portable region surrounding a person that they regard as their own and prefer to keep free from intrusion by others.

optWhy.A: Correct. Personal space is the region surrounding a person kept free from intrusion.
optWhy.B: Not a genetic code.

stem: Hall's proxemics identifies intimate distance as roughly:
why: Hall's intimate distance is roughly 0–45 cm, used for close physical contact and embracing.

optWhy.A: Correct. Intimate distance is roughly 0–45 cm.
optWhy.B: Several kilometres is not intimate distance.

stem: Contact cultures (e.g., Latin American, Mediterranean) generally use:

options.text: Smaller personal distances and more touching than non-contact cultures.

why: Contact cultures use smaller personal distances and more touching, whereas non-contact cultures use larger distances and less touching.

optWhy.A: Correct. Contact cultures use smaller distances and more touching.
optWhy.B: Not genetically fixed distances.

stem: A person stands closer to a friend than to a stranger in a lift. This illustrates:

options.text: Contextual and relational influences on personal space.

why: Personal space varies with context and relationship: people stand closer to friends than to strangers.

optWhy.A: Correct. Contextual and relational influences on personal space.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Invasion of personal space can produce discomfort, arousal, and avoidance.
reason: Personal space serves a regulatory function, and unwanted intrusion threatens a person's sense of control and comfort.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.

why: Both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion: unwanted intrusion into personal space threatens a person's sense of control and comfort, producing discomfort and arousal.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: The reason does explain the assertion.

stem: The distinction between density and crowding is that:

options.text: Density is an objective physical count of people per unit area; crowding is the subjective psychological experience of too little space.

why: Density is an objective physical measure; crowding is the subjective, negative psychological experience of insufficient space.

optWhy.A: Correct. Density is objective physical measure; crowding is subjective psychological experience.
optWhy.B: Density and crowding are not identical.

stem: Two people in a large empty hall may not feel crowded, while four people in a small lift may feel crowded. This illustrates:

options.text: Subjective crowding depends on perceived space and context, not just objective density.
Objective density always equals subjective crowding.

why: Crowding is subjective and depends on perceived space and context, not merely objective density.

optWhy.A: Correct. Subjective crowding depends on perceived space and context.
optWhy.B: Objective density does not always equal subjective crowding.

stem: Psychological consequences of crowding can include:

options.text: Stress, aggression, withdrawal, and reduced task performance.

why: Crowding can produce stress, aggression, social withdrawal, and reduced task performance.

optWhy.A: Correct. Crowding can produce stress, aggression, withdrawal, and reduced task performance.
optWhy.B: Not genetic improvement.

stem: A worker in a noisy, densely packed open-plan office reports stress and reduced concentration. This illustrates:

options.text: Crowding-related stress and environmental stress impairing functioning.

why: Crowding-related stress (density, noise, lack of control) can impair psychological functioning and concentration.

optWhy.A: Correct. Crowding-related stress impairs functioning.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

stem: Crowding tolerance varies across cultures, with some groups tolerating higher densities before experiencing crowding. This illustrates:
why: Crowding tolerance differs across cultures; the same density may be experienced as crowding in one culture but not another.

optWhy.A: Correct. Cultural differences in crowding experiences.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

stem: Territoriality is best defined as:

options.text: The defence and marking of a space that a person or group regards as their own.

why: Territoriality is the behaviour by which people or groups defend and mark a space they regard as their own (e.g., through markers and ownership cues).

optWhy.A: Correct. Territoriality is the defence and marking of one's own space.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

stem: A student puts their name on a desk and places books around it to claim it in a library. This illustrates:

options.text: Territorial marking to signal ownership and control.

why: Using a name and belongings to claim a desk is territorial marking, signalling ownership and control.

optWhy.A: Correct. Territorial marking signals ownership and control.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

stem: Personal territoriality concerns an individual's space, whereas group territoriality concerns:

options.text: A group's defence and marking of a shared space (e.g., a team room or neighbourhood).

why: Group territoriality concerns a group's defence and marking of a shared space, analogous to personal territoriality at the group level.

optWhy.A: Correct. Group territoriality concerns a group's shared space.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

stem: Two neighbours dispute the boundary of their gardens. This illustrates:

options.text: Territoriality and conflict over boundaries and control.

why: Disputes over garden boundaries reflect territoriality and conflict over ownership and control of space.

optWhy.A: Correct. Territoriality and conflict over boundaries and control.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

sub: Applications in residential, institutional and public environments
stem: Designing a prison wing with clear personal cells and limited shared space applies territoriality and crowding principles to:

options.text: Reduce crowding stress and clarify territorial boundaries in an institutional environment.

why: Clear personal cells and limited shared space apply territoriality and crowding principles to reduce crowding stress and clarify boundaries.

optWhy.A: Correct. Applies territoriality and crowding principles to reduce crowding stress and clarify boundaries.
optWhy.B: Not genetic engineering.

stem: Match the classical experiment in List-I with its core finding in List-II.
listII: Informational influence creates emergent group norms
Unanimous majority conformity
High obedience to destructive authority under situational pressure
Insufficient justification produces greater attitude change
Mere categorisation produces in-group favouritism
why: Sherif autokinetic—informational influence creates emergent group norms (1-A). Asch—unanimous majority conformity (2-B). Milgram—high obedience to destructive authority under situational pressure (3-C). Festinger & Carlsmith—insufficient justification produces greater attitude change (4-D). Tajfel minimal group—mere categorisation produces in-group favouritism (5-E).

optWhy.A: Correct. 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D, 5-E.
optWhy.B: The pairings are incorrect.

sub: Cognitive dissonance and attitude change integration
stem: Consider the following statements about cognitive dissonance and attitude change:
statements: I. Insufficient justification produces greater attitude change than sufficient justification.
II. Post-decisional dissonance is reduced by spreading of alternatives.
III. Dissonance only arises from behaviour-behaviour inconsistency, never attitude-behaviour inconsistency.
why: Statements I and II are true. Statement III is false because dissonance commonly arises from attitude-behaviour inconsistency.

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements I and II are true; III is false.
optWhy.B: Statement III is false.

sub: Attribution models applied to complex cross-cultural situations
stem: A manager attributes an employee's failure to laziness, ignoring that the employee lacked resources. Applying Kelley's covariation model, the manager should assess:

options.text: Consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness before attributing the failure to disposition or situation.

why: Kelley's covariation model requires assessing consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness before making a dispositional or situational attribution.

optWhy.A: Correct. Assess consensus, consistency, and distinctiveness.
optWhy.B: Not genetic factors.

key: Attribution models applied to complex situations

sub: Distinction between conformity, compliance and obedience
stem: A teenager adopts friends' slang (conformity), lends money after a friend asks (compliance), and stops at a police officer's command (obedience). This distinguishes:

options.text: Conformity (group norms), compliance (requests), and obedience (authority orders) as distinct forms of social influence.

why: The three behaviours illustrate the distinct forms: conformity to group norms, compliance to a request, and obedience to an authority order.

optWhy.A: Correct. Conformity, compliance, and obedience are distinct forms of social influence.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

sub: Group productivity and social loafing analysis
stem: Consider the following statements about groups:
statements: I. Social loafing is reduced when individual contributions are identifiable.
II. Group cohesion is the same as group productivity.
III. The Ringelmann effect shows individual output declines as group size increases.
why: Statements I and III are true. Statement II is false because cohesion (attraction to the group) is not the same as productivity (actual output).

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements I and III are true; II is false.
optWhy.B: Statement II is false.

stem: Match the leadership theory in List-I with its core idea in List-II.
listII: Leader matches style to follower maturity
Leader clarifies the path to goals and removes obstacles
Leader effectiveness depends on matching leader style to the situation
Leader inspires and transforms followers
why: Fiedler—leader effectiveness depends on matching style to situation (1-C). Hersey-Blanchard—match style to follower maturity (2-A). Path-goal—clarify path and remove obstacles (3-B). Transformational—inspire and transform followers (4-D).

optWhy.A: Correct. 1-C, 2-A, 3-B, 4-D.
optWhy.B: Fiedler is not follower maturity.

stem: A key difference between social identity theory and realistic conflict theory is that:

options.text: SIT derives intergroup bias from categorisation alone, whereas RCT derives it from competition over scarce resources.

why: SIT derives bias from social categorisation and positive distinctiveness (no competition needed); RCT derives hostility from competition over scarce resources.

optWhy.A: Correct. SIT: categorisation; RCT: competition over scarce resources.
optWhy.B: Not genetic predisposition.

sub: Critical evaluation of aggression and prosocial explanations
stem: A child hits a peer after seeing an adult model hit a doll and be rewarded. Applying Bandura's social learning theory, the child learned aggression through:

options.text: Observational learning (modelling), especially when the model is rewarded.

why: Bandura's Bobo doll research showed that children learn aggression through observational learning, especially when the model is rewarded (vicarious reinforcement).

optWhy.A: Correct. Observational learning (modelling), especially when the model is rewarded.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

sub: Application to health, law and environment
stem: A field study finds that households given feedback comparing their energy use to neighbours' reduce consumption. The best interpretation is:

options.text: Descriptive social norms (neighbours' behaviour) can promote pro-environmental behaviour.

why: Feedback comparing one's energy use to neighbours' uses descriptive social norms to promote pro-environmental (energy-conservation) behaviour.

optWhy.A: Correct. Descriptive social norms promote pro-environmental behaviour.
optWhy.B: Not genetic determinism.

stem: Match the applied domain in List-I with a key social-psychological principle in List-II.
listII: Health Belief Model; theory of planned behaviour
Descriptive social norms; pro-environmental behaviour
Eyewitness testimony; misinformation effect
Density versus crowding; territorial markers
why: Health—Health Belief Model and theory of planned behaviour (1-A). Environment—descriptive social norms and pro-environmental behaviour (2-B). Law—eyewitness testimony and misinformation effect (3-C). Personal space/crowding/territoriality—density versus crowding and territorial markers (4-D).

optWhy.A: Correct. 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D.
